title: Revisiting Over-refusal in Safety-aligned Large Language Models: A Representation and Optimization Perspective

paper.title: Revisiting Over-refusal in Safety-aligned Large Language Models: A Representation and Optimization Perspective
paper.abstract:
Abstract. Over-refusal is a critical side effect of safety alignment in large language models (LLMs), causing harmless but superficially risky queries to be mistakenly rejected. Despite the effectiveness of existing mitigation methods, why safety-aligned LLMs may still reject harmless queries under correct safety supervision remains insufficiently understood. To address this gap, we analyze over-refusal through the lens of representation and optimization. We make two observations: 1) the representations of harmful and over-refusal samples are visually distinguishable at certain intermediate layers but increasingly overlap in deeper layers; and 2) harmful-sample gradients exhibit high intra-class similarity and concentrate in a low-rank subspace. Moreover, they are more strongly aligned with refusal-target gradients than with correct helpful-target gradients on over-refusal prompts. This imbalanced gradient coupling can bias over-refusal samples toward refusal, while the reduced apparent representational separation in deeper layers may make it more difficult for the model to maintain a clear boundary between harmful and over-refusal samples.
To this end, we propose GOAL
( G radient O rthogonalization with
contr A stive L earning), a safety-alignment framework for mitigating over-refusal. Specifically, GOAL consists of two components: 1) to prevent imbalanced gradient coupling from biasing
the optimization of over-refusal samples toward refusal, we orthogonalize over-refusal gradients against the low-rank refusal subspace extracted from harmful gradients; and 2) to explicitly
enhance the separation between harmful and over-refusal representations, we introduce a contrastive learning objective. Extensive experiments across multiple models and benchmarks demonstrate that GOAL effectively mitigates over-refusal while preserving safety performance and general capabilities. For reproducibility, we have released the code for GOAL 1 1 1 https://anonymous.4open.science/r/GOAL-C5B1 .

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text: As Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in open-ended, user-facing applications, LLM safety has attracted growing attention ( Brown et al., 2020 ; Achiam et al., 2023 ; Bai et al., 2022 ; Zhai et al., 2026 ; Shi et al., 2026 ; Shao et al., 2026 ) . As a critical side effect of LLM safety, over-refusal, which refers to the mistaken rejection of harmless but superficially risky queries, has been widely studied ( Dabas et al., 2025 ; Lu et al., 2026 ) . To clarify over-refusal, we define three types of samples ( Dabas et al., 2025 ; Lu et al., 2026 ; Cao et al., 2025 ) : harmful samples are genuinely unsafe queries that must be refused; benign samples are clearly harmless queries; and over-refusal samples are harmless but likely to be mistakenly rejected. Existing efforts to mitigate over-refusal can be divided into two lines ( Dabas et al., 2025 ; Lu et al., 2026 ; Cao et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2026 ) . One line aims to reshape the model’s refusal boundary during optimization ( Dabas et al., 2025 ; Lu et al., 2026 ) . For example, DCR introduces a contrastive-refinement stage before safety alignment, encouraging a sharper decision boundary between harmful samples and over-refusal samples ( Lu et al., 2026 ) . The other line of work mitigates over-refusal through targeted interventions ( Cao et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2025 ) . For example, SCANS identifies safety-critical layers and steers their activations with refusal-related directions, suppressing over-refusal while preserving refusals on harmful inputs ( Cao et al., 2025 ) . Despite the effectiveness of existing mitigation methods, why safety-aligned LLMs may still reject harmless queries under correct safety supervision remains insufficiently understood. To address this gap, we analyze over-refusal through the lens of representation and optimization. We make two core observations. 1) Through layer-wise representation visualization, we observe that harmful and over-refusal samples are distinguishable at certain intermediate layers but show increasing overlap as layer depth increases. For example, as shown in Figure 1 , at layer 13, these two types of samples are visually distinguishable in the representation space but increasingly overlap in deeper layers, suggesting a reduction in their apparent representational separation. Such reduced separation may make it more difficult for the model to maintain a clear boundary between harmful and over-refusal samples. 2) Through sample-level gradient statistics, as shown in Figure 2 , we observe that harmful samples exhibit high intra-class gradient similarity during safety alignment, suggesting that their gradients may accumulate coherently and form a low-rank refusal subspace with highly concentrated gradient energy. In contrast, benign and over-refusal samples exhibit low intra-class similarity and more dispersed gradient energy. Moreover, benign sample gradients show low similarity to harmful sample gradients, whereas over-refusal gradients exhibit substantially higher similarity, potentially making the optimization of over-refusal samples more susceptible to the accumulated harmful gradient. Specifically, as shown in Figure 2 (b), harmful sample gradients are more similar to over-refusal-ref gradients than to over-refusal gradients, where over-refusal-ref denotes the gradients induced by pairing over-refusal prompts with refusal targets. This observation suggests that the accumulated harmful gradient is more strongly coupled with the refusal-target gradient than with the correct helpful-target gradient. Such imbalanced gradient coupling may increase the likelihood that the model selects a refusal response during safety alignment. Together, these observations suggest that imbalanced gradient coupling can bias over-refusal samples toward refusal, while reduced apparent representational separation may make it more difficult for the model to maintain a clear boundary between harmful and over-refusal samples. Figure 1 . Layer-wise PCA visualization of last-token representations for benign, harmful, and over-refusal samples in Llama-2-7B-Chat. Notably, harmful and over-refusal samples are visually distinguishable at layer 13 but show increasing overlap in deeper layers. Due to space limitations, representation visualization for an additional model is provided in Appendix E . Figure 2 . Gradient analyses on Llama-2-7B-Chat. (a) Cumulative Explained Ratio (CER) of the top- k k singular values for gradient subspaces of different sample types. (b) Pairwise gradient similarity across different sample types during safety alignment. To this end, we propose GOAL ( G radient O rthogonalization with contr A stive L earning), a safety-alignment framework that utilizes gradient orthogonalization and contrastive learning to mitigate over-refusal. Specifically, GOAL fine-tunes the model on a safety-alignment dataset that includes harmful, benign, and over-refusal samples, while incorporating two complementary components during training. One component aims to mitigate imbalanced gradient coupling that biases the optimization of over-refusal samples toward refusal. Specifically, we orthogonalize over-refusal gradients against a low-rank refusal subspace extracted from harmful gradients. To obtain this subspace, we apply Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) to the per-sample gradients of harmful samples. The other component introduces a contrastive learning objective to explicitly enhance the separation between harmful and over-refusal representations. To balance computational efficiency and over-refusal mitigation, both components are applied by fine-tuning only the selected safety-relevant layers. Extensive experimental results on multiple benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of GOAL in mitigating over-refusal while maintaining safety performance and general capabilities. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: ∙ \bullet We investigate why safety-aligned LLMs still reject harmless over-refusal samples despite correct supervision, identifying increasing visual overlap between harmful and over-refusal representations in deeper layers and a low-rank harmful gradient subspace that aligns more strongly with refusal-target than helpful-target gradients on over-refusal prompts. ∙ \bullet We propose GOAL, a Gradient Orthogonalization with contrAstive Learning framework for mitigating over-refusal. GOAL first extracts a low-rank gradient-based refusal subspace from harmful samples via SVD and orthogonalizes over-refusal gradients against this subspace. It further introduces a contrastive learning objective to enhance the separation between harmful and over-refusal representations. ∙ \bullet Extensive experiments show that GOAL mitigates over-refusal while maintaining safety performance and general capabilities, achieving relative gains of up to 14.03 % 14.03\% in over-refusal mitigation and 1.20 % 1.20\% in safety performance over the second-best methods.

sections.heading: 2.1. Over-refusal in Safety-aligned LLMs
sections.text: As LLMs are increasingly deployed in open-ended and user-facing applications, safety alignment has received widespread attention from the research community ( Zheng et al., 2024 ; Shi et al., 2026 ) . However, while effective in reducing harmful outputs, safety alignment often induces over-refusal, where aligned models reject user requests that appear potentially unsafe but are benign in nature ( Röttger et al., 2024 ; Cui et al., 2024 ; Huang et al., 2024a ) . To better characterize this failure mode, recent studies have introduced dedicated benchmarks that systematically evaluate false refusals across model families and prompt types ( Röttger et al., 2024 ; Shi et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2024 ; Cui et al., 2024 ) . Figure 3 . Overview of the proposed GOAL methodology. Existing efforts to mitigate over-refusal generally fall into two lines ( Dabas et al., 2025 ; Lu et al., 2026 ; Chen et al., 2026 ) . The first line aims to reshape the model’s refusal boundary during optimization ( Dabas et al., 2025 ; Lu et al., 2026 ) . For example, DCR ( Lu et al., 2026 ) introduces a contrastive refinement stage before safety alignment to encourage a sharper decision boundary. The second line focuses on targeted interventions ( Cao et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2025 ) . For example, SCANS ( Cao et al., 2025 ) steers activations in safety-critical layers using refusal steering vectors. Despite their effectiveness, existing methods provide limited understanding of why safety-aligned LLMs trained with correct safety labels may still reject harmless queries.

sections.heading: 2.2. Decision Boundary Shifts in Optimization
sections.text: Decision boundary shift under imbalanced data is an important problem in model optimization ( Hasegawa and Sato, 2024 ; Son et al., 2025 ; Yang et al., 2026 ) . Related studies mainly examine such decision boundary shifts from three perspectives. The first investigates margin-based optimization, where explicit margin objectives or the implicit bias of gradient-based training can enlarge inter-class separation and favor larger-margin solutions ( Schroff et al., 2015 ; Sun et al., 2020 ; Rho et al., 2023 ) . The second focuses on contrastive and metric learning, which reorganize the representation space by pulling positive samples together and pushing negative samples apart, thereby altering the relative geometry of neighboring categories ( Khosla et al., 2020 ; Chen et al., 2020 ; Rho et al., 2023 ) . The third analyzes biased or imbalanced training signals, particularly in long-tailed or imbalanced settings, where differences in class frequency, classifier weights, instance difficulty, or the strength of optimization signals can systematically shift the learned boundary toward particular classes or regions of the representation space ( Hasegawa and Sato, 2024 ; Son et al., 2025 ; Yang et al., 2026 ) . However, the decision boundary perspective has rarely been used to analyze over-refusal, even though over-refusal naturally matches a boundary shift pattern where harmless but safety-sensitive samples are moved toward the refusal side.

sections.heading: 3. Methodology
sections.text: In this section, we propose GOAL ( G radient O rthogonalization with contr A stive L earning), as illustrated in Figure 3 . Specifically, GOAL consists of two complementary components: refusal-orthogonal projection in Section 3.1 and safety-aware contrastive learning in Section 3.2 . Finally, Section 3.3 discusses GOAL.

sections.heading: 3.1. Refusal-orthogonal Projection
sections.text: To prevent imbalanced gradient coupling from attracting over-refusal samples toward the refusal side, we propose refusal-orthogonal projection, which orthogonalizes over-refusal gradients against the refusal subspace. Specifically, we first identify a low-rank refusal subspace from harmful sample gradients. We then explain why over-refusal samples are attracted to this subspace through imbalanced gradient coupling. Based on this analysis, we perform refusal-orthogonal projection to remove the refusal-subspace components from over-refusal gradients, thereby decoupling their optimization from harmful gradients.

sections.heading: 3.1.3. Refusal-orthogonal Projection for Decoupled Optimization
sections.text: Based on the above analysis, there are two natural alternative strategies for mitigating the refusal-subspace attraction effect. One strategy is to downweight harmful gradients, thereby reducing their contribution to the refusal-preference margin of over-refusal samples. However, harmful gradients provide necessary safety supervision, and directly weakening them may compromise the model’s ability to refuse genuinely harmful requests (Appendix R ). Another strategy is to explicitly reduce the coupling between harmful gradients and the counterfactual refusal-target gradients of over-refusal samples. However, during safety alignment, over-refusal samples are paired with their correct helpful responses, and such counterfactual refusal-target gradients are not part of the standard training objective. We therefore adopt a more practical alternative: while fully preserving harmful gradients, we orthogonalize only the available helpful-target gradients of over-refusal samples against the refusal subspace, thereby preventing over-refusal optimization from evolving toward dominant harmful-refusal directions and being attracted to the refusal side. Moreover, our projected update yields a smaller first-order change in the refusal-preference margin than its unprojected counterpart (Appendix L ). sections.heading: 3.2. Safety-aware Contrastive Learning
sections.text: Refusal-orthogonal projection decouples the optimization of over-refusal samples from the refusal subspace, preventing their updates from following dominant harmful-refusal directions. However, controlling the update direction alone does not explicitly specify how harmful and over-refusal samples should be organized in the hidden-state space. To enhance the separability of harmful and over-refusal representations in middle-to-late layers, we introduce a safety-aware contrastive objective. Specifically, we separate the hidden representations of harmful and over-refusal samples with a Circle-style margin contrastive loss ( Sun et al., 2020 ) . Since the final hidden state directly governs token generation, we impose this contrastive constraint at the final layer, thereby obviating the need to enforce contrastive targets across all middle-to-late layers. For each harmful or over-refusal sample in the minibatch ℬ \mathcal{B} , let 𝐡 i \mathbf{h}_{i} denote its last-token hidden state at the final transformer layer. For a given sample, its positive set 𝒫 i \mathcal{P}_{i} and negative set 𝒩 i \mathcal{N}_{i} are constructed from ℳ \mathcal{M} using representations with the same or different labels, respectively. sections.heading: 3.3. Model Discussion
sections.text: We further discuss GOAL. Specifically, we first explain why gradient orthogonalization is necessary beyond contrastive learning, then discuss which layers should be fine-tuned to mitigate over-refusal while improving computational efficiency, and finally analyze the time complexity of GOAL.

sections.heading: 3.3.1. Why contrastive learning alone is insufficient
sections.text: Contrastive learning encourages separation between harmful and over-refusal samples in the hidden-state space, but it does not directly control the SFT gradients that drive parameter updates. Since refusal responses are often highly repetitive, harmful samples can still induce concentrated harmful gradients and bias optimization toward refusal. Therefore, using contrastive learning alone would need to counteract this gradient-level bias only indirectly, which may require a large loss weight and risk harming utility or safety. In contrast, refusal-orthogonal projection directly removes refusal subspace components from over-refusal updates, while contrastive learning further improves representation-level separation. sections.heading: 3.3.2. Choice of Safety-relevant Layers
sections.text: Our objective is to localize the layers responsible for constructing the model’s general safety boundary, as over-refusal can arise when safety-relevant layers misclassify harmless prompts as harmful. Inspired by prior findings ( Cao et al., 2025 ; Dabas et al., 2025 ; Lu et al., 2026 ) , we identify safety-relevant layers using a per-layer separability probe based on hidden-state cosine similarity. Specifically, at each Transformer layer, we compute the within-class similarities of benign–benign and harmful–harmful prompt pairs, as well as the between-class similarity of benign–harmful prompt pairs. We then define a separation gap to quantify the margin between within-class and between-class similarities. This gap widens rapidly across layers because the between-class similarity of benign–harmful pairs drops at a much faster rate than the within-class similarities. We select the contiguous layer block where this gap grows most rapidly as the safety-relevant layers. Notably, the layer where harmful and over-refusal representations are separable in our earlier analysis (Section 1 ) lies near the earlier portion of the identified safety-relevant layers. This pattern suggests that the model initially retains information distinguishing over-refusal samples from harmful ones, but becomes increasingly conservative as safety-relevant representations propagate through deeper layers. Therefore, to improve computational efficiency while mitigating over-refusal, we restrict LoRA fine-tuning to the entire safety-relevant layer block, rather than fine-tuning only the later layers, where our visualization indicates increased overlap between harmful and over-refusal representations. This encourages a coherent safety boundary throughout the layer-wise safety decision process. The refusal-orthogonal projection is applied to the gradients of the trainable parameters in these layers. Meanwhile, the contrastive objective is computed using the final-layer hidden representations, with its gradients backpropagated solely to the trainable LoRA parameters in the selected safety-relevant layers. We defer the full details to Appendix C .

sections.heading: 3.3.3. Time Complexity Analysis
sections.text: Finally, we analyze the computational cost of GOAL. Let d d denote the number of trainable parameters in the selected layers, N N the number of harmful samples used for subspace extraction, k k the number of retained refusal-basis directions, and d h d_{h} the hidden-state dimension. GOAL first performs N N backward passes to collect the harmful gradient matrix 𝐆 ∈ ℝ N × d \mathbf{G}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times d} , and computes the top- k k singular vectors with a truncated SVD, which costs O ⁡ ( N ​ d ​ k ) O(Ndk) . During training, the low-rank projection costs O ⁡ ( B o ​ k ​ d ) O(B_{o}kd) for B o B_{o} over-refusal samples in a minibatch, while the contrastive memory-bank comparison costs O ⁡ ( B c ​ | ℳ | ​ d h ) O(B_{c}|\mathcal{M}|d_{h}) for B c B_{c} contrastive queries. Since k k and | ℳ | |\mathcal{M}| are small, the extra overhead is modest in practice.

sections.text: In this section, we try to answer the following research questions: ∙ \bullet RQ1: How does GOAL perform compared with existing baselines across over-refusal, safety, and general-capability benchmarks (Section 4.2 )? ∙ \bullet RQ2: How does each component of GOAL contribute to the final performance (Section 4.3 )? ∙ \bullet RQ3: Do the selected safety-relevant layers provide an effective target for over-refusal mitigation (Section 4.4 )? ∙ \bullet RQ4: How robust is the extracted low-rank refusal subspace across different extraction settings (Section 4.5 )? ∙ \bullet RQ5: How sensitive is GOAL to key hyperparameters, including the projection rank k k and contrastive loss weight λ \lambda (Section 4.6 )?

sections.heading: 4.1. Experimental Settings
sections.text: Training Data. Our 500-sample training set comprises 200 harmful queries (AdvBench ( Zou et al., 2023 ) , MaliciousInstruct ( Huang et al., 2024b ) , TDC2023 ( Mazeika et al., 2024 ; Mazeika et al., 2023 ) ), 200 benign queries (Alpaca ( Taori et al., 2023 ) ), and 100 over-refusal queries (OR-Bench-Hard ( Cui et al., 2024 ) , XSTest ( Röttger et al., 2024 ) , PHTest ( An et al., 2024 ) ). Reference responses are generated via GPT-4o ( Hurst et al., 2024 ) . Evaluation and Metrics. We evaluate over-refusal via Compliance Rate ( C.R. ) on the held-out test portions of the aforementioned over-refusal datasets, alongside two OOD benchmarks: OKTest ( Shi et al., 2024 ) and CoCoNot ( Brahman et al., 2024 ) . Safety preservation is measured via Safety Score ( S.S. ) on JailbreakBench ( JBB ) ( Chao et al., 2024 ) and STL , our shorthand for a collection of four safety benchmarks from Bianchi et al. (2024) . General capability is assessed via Accuracy ( Acc ) on standard multiple-choice benchmarks (MMLU ( Hendrycks et al., 2020 ) , ARC-C ( Clark et al., 2018 ) , OpenBookQA ( Mihaylov et al., 2018 ) , PIQA ( Bisk et al., 2020 ) ). GPT-5.1 is employed as the judge for evaluating C.R. and S.S. Detailed dataset descriptions, baseline information, metric definitions, training hyperparameters, and implementation details are deferred to Appendix D . Models and Baselines. We evaluate GOAL on Gemma-7B-it, Llama-2-7B-Chat, and Llama-2-13B-Chat ( Touvron et al., 2023 ; Team et al., 2024 ) using greedy decoding. We compare against standard SFT and representative over-refusal mitigation methods, including training-based methods (ACTOR ( Dabas et al., 2025 ) , DCR ( Lu et al., 2026 ) ) and inference-time or representation-level interventions (SCANS ( Cao et al., 2025 ) , Surgical ( Wang et al., 2025 ) ). For a fair comparison, we retrain ACTOR, DCR, and SFT using the same over-refusal data construction strategy as GOAL. Implementation Details. We fine-tune all models with LoRA on the selected safety-relevant layers only, using rank r = 16 r=16 , scaling factor α = 32 \alpha=32 , and dropout rate 0.05 0.05 . The selected layer ranges are layers 12–22 for Llama-2-7B-Chat, layers 13–26 for Llama-2-13B-Chat, and layers 15–23 for Gemma-7B-it. All models are trained for 5 epochs with an effective batch size of 4. We set the refusal-subspace rank to k = 10 k=10 , apply the contrastive loss at the last layer, and use a contrastive weight of λ = 0.1 \lambda=0.1 . The Circle-style contrastive loss uses margin m = 0.25 m=0.25 and scale γ = 80 \gamma=80 , with a class-balanced FIFO memory bank of size 128. sections.heading: 4.2. Overall Performance (RQ1)
sections.text: Table 1 reports the performance of GOAL and the baselines in terms of over-refusal mitigation, safety preservation, and general capability retention across three backbone models. Overall, GOAL achieves leading over-refusal performance while maintaining strong safety and preserving general capabilities. We analyze these three aspects below. Effective mitigation of over-refusal. GOAL consistently attains the highest or second-highest Compliance Rate (C.R.) across all over-refusal benchmarks. Specifically, it achieves the best or tied-best performance on 13 out of 15 over-refusal settings and ranks second on the remaining two. The gains are especially pronounced on challenging OOD benchmarks such as OKTest and CoCoNot. For example, on Llama-2-13B-Chat, GOAL improves OKTest from 0.9400 to 0.9700 and CoCoNot from 0.8496 to 0.8892 compared with the strongest non-GOAL results. These results suggest that GOAL generalizes its mitigation behavior beyond in-domain over-refusal prompts, rather than merely fitting to a specific benchmark distribution. Robust safety preservation. A common failure mode in mitigating over-refusal is the inadvertent degradation of model safety. In contrast, GOAL maintains strong safety performance on both JBB and STL. On Gemma-7B-it, GOAL achieves the best safety scores on both JBB and STL, improving JBB from 0.90 to 0.97 and STL from 0.9748 to 0.9884 compared with the base model. On Llama-2-13B-Chat, GOAL matches the best STL score of 0.9981 while also achieving a competitive JBB score of 0.97. These results show that the improved compliance on over-refusal queries does not come at the cost of substantially weakened safety behavior against genuinely harmful instructions. Maintaining general capabilities. Across all three backbones and four general-capability benchmarks, GOAL largely preserves the performance of the corresponding base models. The largest observed decrease is only 0.0071 0.0071 in absolute accuracy. These results indicate that GOAL mitigates over-refusal without noticeably compromising general capabilities. Further statistical significance analysis and human evaluation are provided in Appendices P and O , respectively.

sections.heading: 5. Conclusion
sections.text: In this work, we analyze over-refusal from both representational and optimization perspectives. Our layer-wise visualization shows that harmful and over-refusal representations are separable at certain intermediate layers but become increasingly entangled in deeper layers. We further find that harmful sample gradients exhibit high intra-class similarity and concentrate in a low-rank subspace, while exhibiting stronger alignment with refusal-target gradients than with helpful-target gradients on over-refusal prompts. Based on these observations, we propose GOAL, which combines refusal-orthogonal projection to decouple over-refusal optimization from harmful gradients with safety-aware contrastive learning to enhance the separation between harmful and over-refusal representations. Extensive experiments across multiple models and benchmarks demonstrate that GOAL substantially mitigates over-refusal while preserving model safety and general capabilities.

sections.heading: Limitations and Ethical Considerations
sections.text: Limitations. Our experiments focus on open-weight instruction-tuned models with 7–13 billion parameters and predominantly English benchmarks. Although the Qwen3-8B results support generalization to a recent model family, further evaluation is needed on larger, proprietary, and multilingual models. Moreover, our first-order analysis provides a sufficient characterization rather than establishing harmful-gradient coupling as the sole cause of over-refusal. Finally, automatic evaluation partly relies on an LLM judge, and strong benchmark performance does not guarantee safety in all deployment settings. Human-evaluation ethics. The human evaluation was conducted by three master’s students, each of whom independently assessed the model responses. The annotators were informed of the study procedure and the possibility of encountering superficially sensitive language, provided informed consent, and could discontinue participation without penalty. They were compensated at a rate of CNY 100 per hour. No personally identifying information was collected, and only aggregate results are reported. Generative-AI assistance. OpenAI Codex was used to assist with language editing, manuscript organization, and LaTeX preparation. The authors made all research decisions, conducted the experiments, and verified the mathematical derivations, numerical results, and citations.

sections.heading: Appendix D Detailed Experimental Settings
sections.text: Models. We evaluate the generalization and robustness of our method on three representative instruction-tuned LLMs: Gemma-7B-it, Llama-2-7B-Chat, and Llama-2-13B-Chat. Greedy decoding is used for all text generation. Training Datasets. To train the models, we construct a dataset 𝒟 train = 𝒟 harmful ∪ 𝒟 benign ∪ 𝒟 over \mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}=\mathcal{D}_{\text{harmful}}\cup\mathcal{D}_{\text{benign}}\cup\mathcal{D}_{\text{over}} , comprising harmful, benign, and over-refusal samples. 𝒟 harmful \mathcal{D}_{\text{harmful}} consists of 200 harmful instructions drawn from AdvBench ( Zou et al., 2023 ) , MaliciousInstruct ( Huang et al., 2024b ) , and TDC2023 ( Mazeika et al., 2024 ; Mazeika et al., 2023 ) . 𝒟 benign \mathcal{D}_{\text{benign}} consists of 200 instructions drawn from the Stanford Alpaca dataset ( Taori et al., 2023 ) , covering a broad range of everyday user intents. 𝒟 over \mathcal{D}_{\text{over}} is compiled by drawing 50 items from OR-Bench-Hard ( Cui et al., 2024 ) and 25 items from each of XSTest ( Röttger et al., 2024 ) and PHTest ( An et al., 2024 ) , yielding 100 prompts whose surface form appears unsafe but whose underlying intent is benign. Reference answers for harmful prompts are aligned refusals, while those for benign and over-refusal prompts are helpful, compliant completions; all reference answers are generated using GPT-4o ( Hurst et al., 2024 ) . Baseline Methods. We compare our proposed GOAL with the following baseline methods: SFT fine-tunes the base model on the aforementioned 𝒟 train \mathcal{D}_{\text{train}} without any additional regularization, serving as the most direct vanilla baseline. ACTOR ( Dabas et al., 2025 ) fine-tunes a single layer to suppress activation components that trigger refusal. DCR ( Lu et al., 2026 ) introduces a preceding contrastive-refinement stage so the model can better distinguish truly toxic from superficially toxic prompts. SCANS ( Cao et al., 2025 ) steers activations in safety-critical layers via refusal steering vectors. Surgical ( Wang et al., 2025 ) ablates a single false-refusal direction in representation space to recover helpful responses on benign samples. Evaluation Datasets. We evaluate over-refusal using the held-out versions of XSTest ( Röttger et al., 2024 ) (225 samples), OR-Bench-Hard ( Cui et al., 2024 ) (1,269 samples), and PHTest ( An et al., 2024 ) (2,052 samples), with OKTest ( Shi et al., 2024 ) (300 samples) and CoCoNot ( Brahman et al., 2024 ) (379 samples) used as out-of-distribution (OOD) benchmarks. To ensure safety preservation, we further evaluate on JailbreakBench (JBB; ( Chao et al., 2024 ) ; 100 samples), targeting adversarial and jailbreak robustness, together with four harmfulness benchmarks from ( Bianchi et al., 2024 ) , collectively denoted as STL in this paper: I-MaliciousInstructions (98 samples), I-CoNa (178 samples), I-Controversial (40 samples), and HarmfulQ ( Shaikh et al., 2023 ) (200 samples)—covering hateful speech, controversial topics, malicious instructions, and common jailbreak prompts (516 samples in total). We assess general model capability using the Language Model Evaluation Harness on multiple-choice benchmarks, including MMLU ( Hendrycks et al., 2020 ) , ARC-Challenge ( Clark et al., 2018 ) , OpenBookQA ( Mihaylov et al., 2018 ) , and PIQA ( Bisk et al., 2020 ) . Data for Representation and Gradient Analyses. We construct balanced diagnostic sets containing 300 and 1,200 samples per category for the representation and gradient analyses, respectively (900 and 3,600 samples in total). The benign samples are drawn from TruthfulQA ( Lin et al., 2022 ) and UltraChat ( Ding et al., 2023 ) ; the over-refusal samples are drawn from PHTest ( An et al., 2024 ) and OR-Bench-Hard ( Cui et al., 2024 ) ; and the harmful samples are drawn from AdvBench ( Zou et al., 2023 ) , Hex-Phi ( Qi et al., 2024 ) , and HH-RLHF ( Bai et al., 2022 ) . These diagnostic sets are used only for the analyses in Figures 1 and 2 and are disjoint from the training and evaluation sets. Metrics. Over-refusal is measured using the Compliance Rate ( C.R. ), defined as the ratio of compliant responses to the total number of generated responses. Similarly, the model’s safety is evaluated with the Safety Score ( S.S. ), calculated as the ratio of safe responses to the total number of responses. Response evaluation for both C.R. and S.S. is conducted using GPT-5.1. For general capability, we report accuracy ( Acc ) on all four multiple-choice benchmarks: for MMLU, this is the overall average accuracy across its 57 subjects; for ARC-Challenge, OpenBookQA, and PIQA, this is the task-level accuracy. Training Hyperparameters and GOAL Implementation. To ensure parameter efficiency, all models are fine-tuned using Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) with a rank of 16 16 , scaling factor α = 32 \alpha=32 , and a dropout rate of 0.05 0.05 . Specifically, we apply LoRA modules exclusively to a selected subset of layers tailored to each model: layers 12–22 for Llama-2-7B-Chat, layers 13–26 for Llama-2-13B-Chat, and layers 15–23 for Gemma-7B-it. During training, we use a micro-batch size of 1 and 4 gradient accumulation steps, resulting in an effective batch size of 4. All models are trained for 5 epochs using bfloat16 precision with a fixed random seed of 42. We apply a warmup ratio of 0.03 0.03 , gradient clipping with a maximum norm of 1.0 1.0 , and no weight decay. For the learning rates, we use 1.75 × 10 − 4 1.75\times 10^{-4} for both Llama-2-7B-Chat and Llama-2-13B-Chat, while a lower learning rate of 2.5 × 10 − 5 2.5\times 10^{-5} is adopted for Gemma-7B-it. For the hyperparameters specific to the GOAL framework, we extract the gradient-based refusal subspace using a projection rank of k = 10 k=10 . The contrastive representation loss is applied at the last layer of each model. The overall loss objective sets the contrastive loss weight to λ = 0.1 \lambda=0.1 . For the circle loss formulation, we set the margin to 0.25 0.25 , the scaling factor to γ = 80 \gamma=80 , and maintain a representation bank ℳ \mathcal{M} of size 128 to facilitate positive and negative pair comparisons. Specifically, rather than using random sampling, we employ an all-to-all deterministic comparison. To strictly control class imbalance, the bank is explicitly partitioned into two independent, class-specific FIFO queues, each with a capacity of 64 (one for harmful representations and one for over-refusal representations). New representations are routed to their respective queues, overwriting the oldest entries. For each query x x , we use all currently available representations in the same-class queue, up to 64, as the positive set 𝒫 x \mathcal{P}_{x} , and all currently available representations in the opposing-class queue, up to 64, as the negative set 𝒩 x \mathcal{N}_{x} . The contrastive loss is then computed directly over this full similarity matrix. Implementation Details of Baselines. For the SFT baseline, we fine-tune the models on 𝒟 train \mathcal{D}_{\text{train}} utilizing exactly the same LoRA configurations, target layer subsets, and training hyperparameters as our GOAL framework. This ensures that any performance improvements are strictly attributable to our proposed mechanisms rather than hyperparameter tuning. For ACTOR , we utilize the same training dataset ( 𝒟 train \mathcal{D}_{\text{train}} ) as GOAL, while keeping its specific optimization hyperparameters and layer configurations identical to those in the original paper ( Dabas et al., 2025 ) . For DCR , which originally leverages 250 samples from XSTest for its contrastive-refinement stage, we maintain an equivalent data scale by sampling 250 instances across OR-Bench-Hard ( Cui et al., 2024 ) , XSTest ( Röttger et al., 2024 ) , and PHTest ( An et al., 2024 ) in accordance with the exact proportional ratio (2:1:1) used for 𝒟 over \mathcal{D}_{\text{over}} , keeping all other training settings unchanged ( Lu et al., 2026 ) . For SCANS ( Cao et al., 2025 ) , the method selects layers based on safety relevance; following the original paper, layers 10–20 are selected for steering in the 7B models, while layers 16–26 are used for the 13B models. Furthermore, we strictly follow the original paper regarding the dataset and hyperparameter designs. Finally, for Surgical ( Wang et al., 2025 ) , we directly apply it using the default configurations and hyperparameters recommended by its original authors. Evaluation Prompts for GPT-5.1 Judge. sections.heading: Appendix H Training Procedure and Runtime Overhead
sections.text: Algorithm 1 summarizes the training procedure of GOAL. We measure its wall-clock cost on Llama-2-7B-Chat using a single NVIDIA A800 GPU with 80GB memory. Under the same training configuration, standard SFT takes 9.53 minutes, while the online training stage of GOAL takes 9.55 minutes, corresponding to an online overhead of only 0.21%. Before training, GOAL performs a one-time refusal-subspace extraction, which takes an additional 2.17 minutes. Therefore, the end-to-end runtime of the first GOAL run is 11.72 minutes, corresponding to a 23.0% overhead relative to standard SFT. The extracted subspace can be reused across repeated training runs that share the same base checkpoint, training data, and trainable parameterization, in which case the one-time preprocessing cost is amortized. We report both online and end-to-end costs to clearly distinguish the training-stage overhead from the complete runtime.

sections.heading: L.2. Empirical Analysis of Refusal Preference Margins
sections.text: We provide likelihood-based empirical evidence for the refusal-margin reduction effect by comparing the base model, vanilla SFT, and the model trained using refusal-orthogonal projection ( Ortho only ). The evaluation is conducted on held-out over-refusal samples that are not used for training or refusal subspace construction. SFT and Ortho only use identical training data, target layers, and optimization hyperparameters, with refusal-orthogonal projection being the only difference. For each over-refusal prompt x i x_{i} , we pair its correct helpful response y i y_{i} with a refusal response y i ′ y_{i}^{\prime} . The refusal preference margin of the i i -th over-refusal sample is then defined as (60) m i ​ ( θ ) = log ⁡ p θ ​ ( y i ′ ∣ x i ) − log ⁡ p θ ​ ( y i ∣ x i ) . m_{i}(\theta)=\log p_{\theta}(y_{i}^{\prime}\mid x_{i})-\log p_{\theta}(y_{i}\mid x_{i}). sections.text: The theoretical analysis of refusal-orthogonal projection is stated in the Euclidean gradient space. AdamW applies an element-wise adaptive preconditioner, which does not necessarily preserve exact Euclidean orthogonality. We therefore examine whether the projected over-refusal gradient remains largely outside the refusal subspace after AdamW preconditioning. Let (69) 𝐮 i , t = ( 𝐈 − 𝐏 ) ​ 𝐠 i , t over \mathbf{u}_{i,t}=(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{P})\mathbf{g}_{i,t}^{\mathrm{over}} denote the projected over-refusal gradient. By construction, 𝐏𝐮 i , t = 𝟎 \mathbf{P}\mathbf{u}_{i,t}=\mathbf{0} . Let (70) 𝐃 t = diag ⁡ ( 1 𝐯 ^ t + ϵ ) \mathbf{D}_{t}=\operatorname{diag}\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{\widehat{\mathbf{v}}_{t}}+\epsilon}\right) denote the diagonal second-moment preconditioner used by AdamW. sections.heading: Appendix O Human Evaluation and Response-Quality Analysis
sections.text: The primary evaluation in our experiments uses GPT-5.1 to determine whether a model response constitutes an unwarranted refusal. Although this evaluation directly measures over-refusal, a non-refusal response is not necessarily correct, helpful, or complete. We therefore conduct an additional response-quality evaluation using both GPT-5.1 and human annotators. This analysis examines whether the reduction in refusal achieved by GOAL corresponds to genuinely useful responses and whether the GPT-5.1 evaluation is broadly consistent with human judgments.

sections.heading: O.1. Evaluation Setup
sections.text: We randomly sample N human = 200 N_{\mathrm{human}}=200 prompts from the held-out over-refusal evaluation sets. For each prompt, we collect responses generated by vanilla SFT, ACTOR, which is the strongest competing method on this backbone in our main experiments, and GOAL. All methods use the same decoding configuration, including the temperature, maximum generation length, and sampling parameters. To reduce potential presentation bias, model identities and method names are hidden during evaluation, and the responses are randomly shuffled for each prompt. The same prompt–response pairs are evaluated by GPT-5.1 and human annotators, enabling a direct comparison between the two evaluation procedures. Each response is evaluated along the following dimensions: ∙ \bullet Unwarranted refusal : whether the model refuses, evades, or unnecessarily avoids answering a benign request. ∙ \bullet Helpfulness : the extent to which the response addresses the user’s request and provides useful information, measured on a five-point Likert scale. ∙ \bullet Correctness : the factual and logical correctness of the response, measured on a five-point Likert scale. ∙ \bullet Completeness : whether the response sufficiently addresses the important aspects of the request, measured on a five-point Likert scale. We additionally define Useful Compliance as (79) UC i = 𝕀 [ r i = 0 ∧ h i ≥ 4 ∧ c i ≥ 4 ] , \mathrm{UC}_{i}=\mathbb{I}\left[r_{i}=0\;\land\;h_{i}\geq 4\;\land\;c_{i}\geq 4\right], where r i r_{i} indicates an unwarranted refusal, and h i h_{i} and c i c_{i} denote the helpfulness and correctness scores, respectively. The overall Useful Compliance rate is defined as (80) UC = 1 N human ​ ∑ i = 1 N human UC i . \mathrm{UC}=\frac{1}{N_{\mathrm{human}}}\sum_{i=1}^{N_{\mathrm{human}}}\mathrm{UC}_{i}. This metric prevents a response from being counted as successful merely because it does not explicitly refuse. A high Useful Compliance rate requires the response to be both non-refusing and substantively useful.

sections.heading: O.2. GPT-5.1 Quality Evaluation
sections.text: In addition to the binary refusal judgment used in the main experiments, we ask GPT-5.1 to evaluate the helpfulness, correctness, and completeness of each response. The evaluator is provided with the original prompt and the corresponding model response but is not given the identity of the evaluated method. The GPT-5.1 evaluator first determines whether the response contains an unwarranted refusal and then assigns an integer score from 1 1 to 5 5 for each quality dimension. A score of 1 1 indicates that the response is severely deficient, whereas a score of 5 5 indicates that it fully satisfies the corresponding criterion. We use a fixed evaluation prompt and deterministic decoding to improve evaluation consistency.

sections.heading: O.3. Human Evaluation
sections.text: Each prompt–response pair is independently evaluated by three human annotators. The annotators are given the same definitions of unwarranted refusal, helpfulness, correctness, and completeness as the GPT-5.1 evaluator. They are blind to both the method identity and the GPT-5.1 judgment. Non-refusal requires unanimous agreement among the three annotators; otherwise, the response is counted as refusal, while quality ratings are averaged. Across all 600 prompt–response pairs, agreement is substantial (Fleiss’ κ = 0.71 \kappa=0.71 ; ordinal Krippendorff’s α = 0.75 \alpha=0.75 – 0.81 0.81 ). The GPT-5.1 and human evaluations are performed on exactly the same responses, allowing us to examine whether the conclusions obtained using the automated evaluator are consistent with those obtained from human assessment. sections.heading: O.4. Results
sections.text: As shown in Table 10 , GOAL consistently achieves the lowest unwarranted-refusal rate under both GPT-5.1 and human evaluation. According to GPT-5.1, GOAL reduces the refusal rate from 19.5 % 19.5\% for SFT and 14.5 % 14.5\% for ACTOR to 9.0 % 9.0\% . Human annotators report the same trend, with refusal rates of 21.5 % 21.5\% , 15.0 % 15.0\% , and 10.0 % 10.0\% for SFT, ACTOR, and GOAL, respectively. More importantly, the reduction in refusal is accompanied by improved response quality. GOAL obtains the highest helpfulness, correctness, and completeness scores under both evaluation procedures. Under human evaluation, GOAL achieves a Useful Compliance rate of 76.0 % 76.0\% , compared with 66.5 % 66.5\% for SFT and 70.0 % 70.0\% for ACTOR. This indicates that GOAL does not reduce over-refusal merely by replacing refusals with perfunctory or low-quality responses. The GPT-5.1 and human evaluations also produce consistent method-level conclusions: both evaluators rank GOAL first across all reported metrics, and the corresponding refusal rates and quality scores follow similar trends. These results provide additional evidence for the reliability of the GPT-5.1-based evaluation used in our main experiments while confirming that the improvement in over-refusal is accompanied by genuinely useful responses.

sections.heading: Appendix Q Comparison with Alternative Gradient Intervention Strategies
sections.text: To determine whether the improvement of GOAL can be reproduced by generic gradient surgery or rank-one gradient removal, we compare the proposed low-rank projection with two alternative gradient intervention strategies: PCGrad and harmful mean-gradient orthogonalization. This comparison examines whether explicitly modeling the low-rank structure of harmful per-sample gradients is necessary for mitigating over-refusal. PCGrad. PCGrad ( Yu et al., 2020 ) is a general multi-objective gradient surgery method designed to resolve negative interference between task gradients. We treat the harmful, benign, and over-refusal objectives as three training objectives. We follow the standard PCGrad procedure and randomize the order of pairwise gradient projections at each optimization step. Unlike GOAL, PCGrad operates on aggregated objective gradients and applies projection only when conventional negative gradient interference is detected. Harmful mean-gradient orthogonalization. We additionally consider a rank-one projection baseline constructed from the mean harmful gradient. Over-refusal is a critical side effect of safety alignment in large language models (LLMs), causing harmless but superficially risky queries to be mistakenly rejected. Despite the effectiveness of existing mitigation methods, why safety-aligned LLMs may still reject harmless queries under correct safety supervision remains insufficiently understood. To address this gap, we analyze over-refusal through the lens of representation and optimization. We make two observations: 1) the representations of harmful and over-refusal samples are visually distinguishable at certain intermediate layers but increasingly overlap in deeper layers; and 2) harmful-sample gradients exhibit high intra-class similarity and concentrate in a low-rank subspace. Moreover, they are more strongly aligned with refusal-target gradients than with correct helpful-target gradients on over-refusal prompts. This imbalanced gradient coupling can bias over-refusal samples toward refusal, while the reduced apparent representational separation in deeper layers may make it more difficult for the model to maintain a clear boundary between harmful and over-refusal samples. To this end, we propose GOAL ( G radient O rthogonalization with contr A stive L earning), a safety-alignment framework for mitigating over-refusal. Specifically, GOAL consists of two components: 1) to prevent imbalanced gradient coupling from biasing the optimization of over-refusal samples toward refusal, we orthogonalize over-refusal gradients against the low-rank refusal subspace extracted from harmful gradients; and 2) to explicitly enhance the separation between harmful and over-refusal representations, we introduce a contrastive learning objective. Extensive experiments across multiple models and benchmarks demonstrate that GOAL effectively mitigates over-refusal while preserving safety performance and general capabilities. Introduction As Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in open-ended, user-facing applications, LLM safety has attracted growing attention ( Brown et al., 2020 ; Achiam et al., 2023 ; Bai et al., 2022 ; Zhai et al., 2026 ; Shi et al., 2026 ; Shao et al., 2026 ) . As a critical side effect of LLM safety, over-refusal, which refers to the mistaken rejection of harmless but superficially risky queries, has been widely studied ( Dabas et al., 2025 ; Lu et al., 2026 ) . To clarify over-refusal, we define three types of samples ( Dabas et al., 2025 ; Lu et al., 2026 ; Cao et al., 2025 ) : harmful samples are genuinely unsafe queries that must be refused; benign samples are clearly harmless queries; and over-refusal samples are harmless but likely to be mistakenly rejected. Existing efforts to mitigate over-refusal can be divided into two lines ( Dabas et al., 2025 ; Lu et al., 2026 ; Cao et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2026 ) . One line aims to reshape the model’s refusal boundary during optimization ( Dabas et al., 2025 ; Lu et al., 2026 ) . For example, DCR introduces a contrastive-refinement stage before safety alignment, encouraging a sharper decision boundary between harmful samples and over-refusal samples ( Lu et al., 2026 ) . The other line of work mitigates over-refusal through targeted interventions ( Cao et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2025 ) . For example, SCANS identifies safety-critical layers and steers their activations with refusal-related directions, suppressing over-refusal while preserving refusals on harmful inputs ( Cao et al., 2025 ) . Despite the effectiveness of existing mitigation methods, why safety-aligned LLMs may still reject harmless queries under correct safety supervision remains insufficiently understood. To address this gap, we analyze over-refusal through the lens of representation and optimization. We make two core observations. 1) Through layer-wise representation visualization, we observe that harmful and over-refusal samples are distinguishable at certain intermediate layers but show increasing overlap as layer depth increases. For example, as shown in Figure 1 , at layer 13, these two types of samples are visually distinguishable in the representation space but increasingly overlap in deeper layers, suggesting a reduction in their apparent representational separation. Such reduced separation may make it more difficult for the model to maintain a clear boundary between harmful and over-refusal samples. 2) Through sample-level gradient statistics, as shown in Figure 2 , we observe that harmful samples exhibit high intra-class gradient similarity during safety alignment, suggesting that their gradients may accumulate coherently and form a low-rank refusal subspace with highly concentrated gradient energy. In contrast, benign and over-refusal samples exhibit low intra-class similarity and more dispersed gradient energy. Moreover, benign sample gradients show low similarity to harmful sample gradients, whereas over-refusal gradients exhibit substantially higher similarity, potentially making the optimization of over-refusal samples more susceptible to the accumulated harmful gradient. Specifically, as shown in Figure 2 (b), harmful sample gradients are more similar to over-refusal-ref gradients than to over-refusal gradients, where over-refusal-ref denotes the gradients induced by pairing over-refusal prompts with refusal targets. This observation suggests that the accumulated harmful gradient is more strongly coupled with the refusal-target gradient than with the correct helpful-target gradient. Such imbalanced gradient coupling may increase the likelihood that the model selects a refusal response during safety alignment. Together, these observations suggest that imbalanced gradient coupling can bias over-refusal samples toward refusal, while reduced apparent representational separation may make it more difficult for the model to maintain a clear boundary between harmful and over-refusal samples. To this end, we propose GOAL ( G radient O rthogonalization with contr A stive L earning), a safety-alignment framework that utilizes gradient orthogonalization and contrastive learning to mitigate over-refusal. Specifically, GOAL fine-tunes the model on a safety-alignment dataset that includes harmful, benign, and over-refusal samples, while incorporating two complementary components during training. One component aims to mitigate imbalanced gradient coupling that biases the optimization of over-refusal samples toward refusal. Extensive experimental results on multiple benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of GOAL in mitigating over-refusal while maintaining safety performance and general capabilities. Related Works 2.1. Over-refusal in Safety-aligned LLMs As LLMs are increasingly deployed in open-ended and user-facing applications, safety alignment has received widespread attention from the research community ( Zheng et al., 2024 ; Shi et al., 2026 ) . However, while effective in reducing harmful outputs, safety alignment often induces over-refusal, where aligned models reject user requests that appear potentially unsafe but are benign in nature ( Röttger et al., 2024 ; Cui et al., 2024 ; Huang et al., 2024a ) . To better characterize this failure mode, recent studies have introduced dedicated benchmarks that systematically evaluate false refusals across model families and prompt types ( Röttger et al., 2024 ; Shi et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2024 ; Cui et al., 2024 ) . Figure 3 . Overview of the proposed GOAL methodology. Existing efforts to mitigate over-refusal generally fall into two lines ( Dabas et al., 2025 ; Lu et al., 2026 ; Chen et al., 2026 ) . The first line aims to reshape the model’s refusal boundary during optimization ( Dabas et al., 2025 ; Lu et al., 2026 ) . For example, DCR ( Lu et al., 2026 ) introduces a contrastive refinement stage before safety alignment to encourage a sharper decision boundary. The second line focuses on targeted interventions ( Cao et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2025 ) . For example, SCANS ( Cao et al., 2025 ) steers activations in safety-critical layers using refusal steering vectors. Despite their effectiveness, existing methods provide limited understanding of why safety-aligned LLMs trained with correct safety labels may still reject harmless queries. 2.2. Decision Boundary Shifts in Optimization Decision boundary shift under imbalanced data is an important problem in model optimization ( Hasegawa and Sato, 2024 ; Son et al., 2025 ; Yang et al., 2026 ) . Related studies mainly examine such decision boundary shifts from three perspectives. The first investigates margin-based optimization, where explicit margin objectives or the implicit bias of gradient-based training can enlarge inter-class separation and favor larger-margin solutions ( Schroff et al., 2015 ; Sun et al., 2020 ; Rho et al., 2023 ) . The second focuses on contrastive and metric learning, which reorganize the representation space by pulling positive samples together and pushing negative samples apart, thereby altering the relative geometry of neighboring categories ( Khosla et al., 2020 ; Chen et al., 2020 ; Rho et al., 2023 ) . The third analyzes biased or imbalanced training signals, particularly in long-tailed or imbalanced settings, where differences in class frequency, classifier weights, instance difficulty, or the strength of optimization signals can systematically shift the learned boundary toward particular classes or regions of the representation space ( Hasegawa and Sato, 2024 ; Son et al., 2025 ; Yang et al., 2026 ) . However, the decision boundary perspective has rarely been used to analyze over-refusal, even though over-refusal naturally matches a boundary shift pattern where harmless but safety-sensitive samples are moved toward the refusal side. 3. Specifically, we first explain why gradient orthogonalization is necessary beyond contrastive learning, then discuss which layers should be fine-tuned to mitigate over-refusal while improving computational efficiency, and finally analyze the time complexity of GOAL. 3.3.1. Why contrastive learning alone is insufficient Contrastive learning encourages separation between harmful and over-refusal samples in the hidden-state space, but it does not directly control the SFT gradients that drive parameter updates. Since refusal responses are often highly repetitive, harmful samples can still induce concentrated harmful gradients and bias optimization toward refusal. Therefore, using contrastive learning alone would need to counteract this gradient-level bias only indirectly, which may require a large loss weight and risk harming utility or safety. In contrast, refusal-orthogonal projection directly removes refusal subspace components from over-refusal updates, while contrastive learning further improves representation-level separation. Choice of Safety-relevant Layers Our objective is to localize the layers responsible for constructing the model’s general safety boundary, as over-refusal can arise when safety-relevant layers misclassify harmless prompts as harmful. Inspired by prior findings ( Cao et al., 2025 ; Dabas et al., 2025 ; Lu et al., 2026 ) , we identify safety-relevant layers using a per-layer separability probe based on hidden-state cosine similarity. Specifically, at each Transformer layer, we compute the within-class similarities of benign–benign and harmful–harmful prompt pairs, as well as the between-class similarity of benign–harmful prompt pairs. We then define a separation gap to quantify the margin between within-class and between-class similarities. This gap widens rapidly across layers because the between-class similarity of benign–harmful pairs drops at a much faster rate than the within-class similarities. We select the contiguous layer block where this gap grows most rapidly as the safety-relevant layers. Notably, the layer where harmful and over-refusal representations are separable in our earlier analysis (Section 1 ) lies near the earlier portion of the identified safety-relevant layers. This pattern suggests that the model initially retains information distinguishing over-refusal samples from harmful ones, but becomes increasingly conservative as safety-relevant representations propagate through deeper layers. Therefore, to improve computational efficiency while mitigating over-refusal, we restrict LoRA fine-tuning to the entire safety-relevant layer block, rather than fine-tuning only the later layers, where our visualization indicates increased overlap between harmful and over-refusal representations. This encourages a coherent safety boundary throughout the layer-wise safety decision process. The refusal-orthogonal projection is applied to the gradients of the trainable parameters in these layers. Meanwhile, the contrastive objective is computed using the final-layer hidden representations, with its gradients backpropagated solely to the trainable LoRA parameters in the selected safety-relevant layers. Experimental Settings Training Data. Our 500-sample training set comprises 200 harmful queries (AdvBench ( Zou et al., 2023 ) , MaliciousInstruct ( Huang et al., 2024b ) , TDC2023 ( Mazeika et al., 2024 ; Mazeika et al., 2023 ) ), 200 benign queries (Alpaca ( Taori et al., 2023 ) ), and 100 over-refusal queries (OR-Bench-Hard ( Cui et al., 2024 ) , XSTest ( Röttger et al., 2024 ) , PHTest ( An et al., 2024 ) ). Reference responses are generated via GPT-4o ( Hurst et al., 2024 ) . Evaluation and Metrics. We evaluate over-refusal via Compliance Rate ( C.R. ) on the held-out test portions of the aforementioned over-refusal datasets, alongside two OOD benchmarks: OKTest ( Shi et al., 2024 ) and CoCoNot ( Brahman et al., 2024 ) . Safety preservation is measured via Safety Score ( S.S. ) on JailbreakBench ( JBB ) ( Chao et al., 2024 ) and STL , our shorthand for a collection of four safety benchmarks from Bianchi et al. (2024) . General capability is assessed via Accuracy ( Acc ) on standard multiple-choice benchmarks (MMLU ( Hendrycks et al., 2020 ) , ARC-C ( Clark et al., 2018 ) , OpenBookQA ( Mihaylov et al., 2018 ) , PIQA ( Bisk et al., 2020 ) ). GPT-5.1 is employed as the judge for evaluating C.R. and S.S. Detailed dataset descriptions, baseline information, metric definitions, training hyperparameters, and implementation details are deferred to Appendix D . Models and Baselines. We evaluate GOAL on Gemma-7B-it, Llama-2-7B-Chat, and Llama-2-13B-Chat ( Touvron et al., 2023 ; Team et al., 2024 ) using greedy decoding. We compare against standard SFT and representative over-refusal mitigation methods, including training-based methods (ACTOR ( Dabas et al., 2025 ) , DCR ( Lu et al., 2026 ) ) and inference-time or representation-level interventions (SCANS ( Cao et al., 2025 ) , Surgical ( Wang et al., 2025 ) ). For a fair comparison, we retrain ACTOR, DCR, and SFT using the same over-refusal data construction strategy as GOAL. Implementation Details. We fine-tune all models with LoRA on the selected safety-relevant layers only, using rank r = 16 r=16 , scaling factor α = 32 \alpha=32 , and dropout rate 0.05 0.05 . The selected layer ranges are layers 12–22 for Llama-2-7B-Chat, layers 13–26 for Llama-2-13B-Chat, and layers 15–23 for Gemma-7B-it. All models are trained for 5 epochs with an effective batch size of 4. We set the refusal-subspace rank to k = 10 k=10 , apply the contrastive loss at the last layer, and use a contrastive weight of λ = 0.1 \lambda=0.1 . The Circle-style contrastive loss uses margin m = 0.25 m=0.25 and scale γ = 80 \gamma=80 , with a class-balanced FIFO memory bank of size 128.
